metadata.document: SUBMISSION ON DISCUSSION DOCUMENT “FRESHWATER FARM PLAN REGULATIONS”
metadata.organisation: Choose Clean Water (Environmental Defence Society Inc, Fish and Game Council, Greenpeace Aotearoa, Royal Forest and Bird Protection Society of New Zealand)

cleaned_body_text: This is a submission on the discussion document “Freshwater farm plan regulations”, Publication Number ME 1577 (Discussion Document). The Discussion Document seeks feedback on the regulations needed to give effect to the freshwater farm plan process set out in Part 9A of the Resource Management Act 1991 (RMA). Environmental Defence Society (EDS), Greenpeace, Fish and Game, and Forest & Bird have a long-standing interest in the management of freshwater in Aotearoa New Zealand. The state of freshwater is well documented and under threat, with half of New Zealand’s river length in pastoral catchments and polluted with nutrients, pathogens and suspended sediment. In respect of freshwater farm plans, the collective vision of the organisations is largely aligned, setting out a joint position in this submission. The Discussion Document sets options for the content of freshwater farm plans, how they will be certified and audited, and the approach for implementation. As freshwater farm plans are intended to provide an alternative pathway for achieving national or regional regulations, it is essential that they are robustly tested and capable of achieving regulated outcomes. Key concerns must be addressed, including a clear line of sight between national policy, regional plan objectives, targets and rules, and freshwater farm plans. Regional plans must include clear, unambiguous rules, and outcomes to be achieved on-farm must be specified in regulation rather than unenforceable guidance documents. Freshwater farm plans should include meaningful base information, and actions to avoid, mitigate or remedy risks must be sufficiently detailed with implementation timeframes. Certification and audit processes should be owned by the regional council to reduce the risk of client capture and enable a catchment-wide approach. Government should anticipate ways for-profit companies could exploit the farm planning regime to protect the public interest, and freshwater farm plans should be publicly available with commercially sensitive information redacted. The roll-out should occur as soon as possible on a catchment-by-catchment basis, prioritising catchments approaching tipping points. The submission details context from past farm planning failures such as the 2003 Dairying and Clean Streams Accord and the 2013 Sustainable Dairying Accord, emphasizing that industry-driven attempts failed due to a lack of regulatory oversight, poorly determined nutrient management budgets, and a focus on outputs while ignoring excessively high farm system inputs like fertilizer and imported feedstock. It also reviews the Canterbury Farm Environment Plan (FEP) system as a cautionary case study. Regarding the content of freshwater farm plans, the organisations support Option 2 for regulated outcomes as it provides necessary specificity, while noting that terms like “minimise”, “adequate”, and “appropriate” introduce ambiguity. Regulated base information should reflect Te Mana o te Wai and provide paddock-scale maps to identify risks and mitigations. For actions, a template methodology such as a National Freshwater Assessment Tool should be used to ensure consistency, and avoidance should explicitly include intensity reductions through input management (e.g., reductions in synthetic nitrogen fertilizer and imported feedstock like Palm Kernel Extract). Option 3 is supported to ensure high-risk activities have highly prescribed actions rather than relying on professional judgement. Timeframes must be built in with a staged approach requiring continuous improvement. For certification and auditing, both processes should be housed within regional councils to maintain accountability, connect with regional plan rules, and enable catchment-scale insights. Certifiers and auditors should be appointed by regional councils with costs recovered from farmers, and central government agencies should audit the regional councils' audit functions. Independent accreditation bodies tied to industry groups (such as the Fertiliser Association or dairy companies) create serious risks of client capture and conflicts of interest. Freshwater farm plans should be publicly available on regional council websites once certified, mirroring resource consents. Enforcement provisions should be strengthened with higher financial penalties, and non-compliant farm systems should default to standard operating procedures like resource consent processes. Finally, the roll-out of freshwater farm plans must occur urgently, utilizing a catchment-by-catchment approach and prioritizing areas experiencing rapid land use change and declining water quality such as the Canterbury High Country.
